title: Recall scaling decisions and limits
summary: Apply the same scaling facts to longer operational prompts without choices. Per-rule stabilization is not a global freeze, and a capacity limit does not prove useful application performance.

up.clue: A single-process workload needs more RAM and cannot divide this work among extra machines. Name the direction that increases the existing instance’s capacity.

down.clue: The same machine now needs less CPU and memory, and the operator reduces its size without removing an instance. Name this scaling direction.

out.clue: A service keeps its per-worker size but adds workers to distribute a sustained backlog. Name this scaling direction.

in.clue: Demand has fallen, remaining workers can handle it, and departing workers finish their requests before removal. Name the direction that reduces the instance count.

automatic.clue: A controller observes load and applies configured rules to add or remove capacity as needed. Name this automated resource-adjustment process.

cooldown.clue: A rule has acted and its stabilization interval prevents that rule from acting again immediately; another rule is evaluated independently. Name the setting for that interval. Use the single-word duration-setting term.

minimum.clue: A request to remove more replicas would cross the profile’s lower capacity boundary. Name the setting defining that boundary, rather than the fallback used when metrics fail. Use a label ending in instance count.

maximum.clue: A requested expansion exceeds the configured profile’s permitted upper capacity. Name the setting that bounds how many instances it may allocate. Use a label ending in instance count.
